cues.text: I agree with Justice Sotomayor's discussion of the Alien Tort Statute.
But I think the Court is correct to conclude that the Torture Victim Protection Act of 1991 (TVPA) does not encompass aiding-and-abetting liability.

I write separately because, while my textual analysis of the TVPA tracks the majority's, I do not agree with how the majority deploys Central Bank of Denver, N. A. v. First Interstate Bank of Denver, N. A. here.
Central Bank is relevant insofar as it instructs that “there is no general presumption” that a statute imposes aiding-and-abetting liability; rather, Congress must provide it.
And here, Congress's use of the term “subjects” does not do so.
But, as Justice Sotomayor discusses, the majority is wrong to treat Central Bank as creating a “magic words” test for aiding-and-abetting liability generally.
(“We have so often denounced” a “ `magic words' test”).
Instead, the absence of the words “aid” and “abet” in the statute we interpreted in Central Bank was but one consideration of many.
I therefore concur only in the judgment as to the majority's TVPA holding.
